title: Income, expenses, saving and investing.
subtitle: Four basic concepts that build the whole of personal finance.
openingQuestion: Person A earns 30 million a month and saves 3 million. Person B earns 15 million and saves 4 million. Who has the stronger financial footing?
openingOptions: Person B, because their savings rate is higher (27% versus 10%)
The same, because both are able to save something
Person B, because they save more in absolute terms in every single month
Person A, because their income is higher
explanation: The savings rate matters more than the absolute amount, because it drives both sides of the equation: how much you set aside each month, and how much you need to live on. Person B saves 27% of income, person A only 10% - that gap is not just faster accumulation, it's also a lower lifestyle to sustain, so the destination is closer too. This is why raising income while spending rises to match it barely shortens the journey at all.

diagram.label: Put savings to work by investing them

realWorldExample.description: An income of VND 20m a month splits into: VND 10m for needs - rent, food, transport, insurance; VND 6m for wants - eating out, entertainment, shopping; VND 4m for saving and debt repayment. Where the rule is most often misread is the first part: if rent alone is already VND 10m, the problem is not spending discipline but fixed costs, and cutting coffee will not fix it. The rule is not there to be obeyed exactly, it is there to show which part is swelling - and the part that swells usually matters more than the other two combined.

quiz.question: What is the difference between saving and investing?
options: Saving preserves capital; investing accepts risk in exchange for a return
Saving only means a bank account; investing only means stocks
Investing preserves capital, while saving is what accepts risk
Both preserve capital equally; they differ only in interest rate
quiz.explanation: Saving preserves capital, and the interest rate is usually below inflation. Investing accepts risk in exchange for a higher return, aiming to grow real wealth.

quiz.question: Which of these is a variable cost?
options: Money spent on clothes shopping, as the need arises
Tuition paid at a fixed amount each semester
Rent paid at a fixed amount every month
A fixed monthly instalment on a bank loan
quiz.explanation: A variable cost changes with your behaviour and needs. Rent and loan instalments are fixed costs. Clothes shopping depends on your own decisions each month.

quiz.question: Scenario: Your income is 20 million a month. Fixed costs (rent, loan instalment, utilities): 12 million. Variable costs (food, shopping, entertainment): 5 million. What is your current savings rate? If variable costs drop to 3 million, what is the new savings rate?
options: Currently 25%, new rate 30% (dividing by costs instead)
Currently 15%, new rate 25% (3/20, then 5/20)
Currently 15%, new rate 20% (only 1 million counted as saved)
Currently 20%, new rate 25% (forgetting the utilities)
quiz.explanation: Currently: (20 − 12 − 5) / 20 = 3 / 20 = 15%. New: (20 − 12 − 3) / 20 = 5 / 20 = 25%. Cutting variable costs by 2 million raises the savings rate from 15% to 25%.

quiz.question: Scenario: Income is 20 million, savings 4 million. A few years later income rises to 40 million, savings to 6 million. How has the savings rate changed?
options: It hasn't changed, since both sides rose together
It rose from 20% to 30%, because more is being saved
It fell from 20% to 15%, even though the amount saved rose
It fell from 20% to 10% (= 4 ÷ 40)
quiz.explanation: 4 ÷ 20 = 20%, while 6 ÷ 40 = 15%. The amount saved rose by 2 million, yet the rate fell - this is a lifestyle inflating in step with income, and because a financial goal is measured in years of spending saved up, it's the new, lower rate that decides how far away the goal is.

quiz.question: Which of these is a fixed cost?
options: Money spent on gifts around holidays and special occasions
Eating out, which varies month to month
Petrol, which depends on distance travelled
Rent paid monthly under a lease contract
quiz.explanation: A fixed cost doesn't change with how much you do in a given month: whether you travel a lot or a little, rent stays the same. Telling the two groups apart decides where to cut - trimming the variable group is visible right away, but the fixed group is where the most money actually flows out.

keyTakeaways: The savings rate matters more than the absolute amount saved
Saving preserves capital; investing grows it through calculated risk
Telling fixed costs apart from variable costs is how you control a budget

practicePrompt.question: If your income is 20 million a month and fixed costs are 12 million, what should you prioritise first to strengthen your financial footing?
options: Cut variable expenses and raise the savings rate
Skip planning altogether, since the amount left over is small
Increase spending on entertainment
Borrow more to have more to spend
practicePrompt.explanation: Controlling variable costs is the fastest way to raise your savings rate without needing to raise income right away.

summary.keyIdea: Saving is the foundation; investing is the next step once that foundation is solid.
summary.commonMistake: Judging financial strength by income rather than by savings rate.
summary.action: Work out your own savings rate for this month and set a goal to nudge it up by 5%.

application.title: Apply it now
application.message: Look back at three variable expenses this month and ask: which one could shrink without meaningfully hurting your quality of life?

sections.text: Person A earns 30 million a month and saves 3 million. Person B earns 15 million and saves 4 million. Who has the stronger financial footing? The answer turns on one number few people pay attention to: the savings rate.

Personal finance is built on four concepts: income (money in), expenses (money out), saving (income minus expenses, holding its value unchanged) and investing (putting savings into assets that earn a return, accepting risk to grow). The four are tightly linked: without income exceeding expenses there is nothing to save, and without saving there is no capital to invest.
Why does the rate matter more than the absolute number?

Person A saves 3/30 = 10% of income. Person B saves 4/15 ≈ 27% of income. Even though B's absolute amount is smaller than A's, B's savings rate is 2.7 times higher. Over the long run, it is this rate - not absolute income - that drives the pace of wealth accumulation, because the rate reflects spending discipline, something a person controls fully regardless of whether their income is high or low.

items: Fixed costs: rent, insurance, loan instalments - unchanged whether you spend a lot or a little that month
Variable costs: food, entertainment, shopping - shift with daily habits and choices
Telling the two apart tells you exactly what can be trimmed when the savings rate needs to rise

sections.label: Saving versus investing
sections.text: Saving preserves capital (a bank deposit, holding cash) - safe, but barely growing in real terms after inflation. Investing accepts calculated risk to grow capital over time. A solid financial foundation needs both, not just one.

lines: A high income is an advantage, but not a sufficient condition. The savings rate - which anyone can control - is the real foundation of personal finance.
